title: Microscope Slides in Motion — source and archive registry supplement 09

records.institution: Harvard University — Museum of Comparative Zoology and Countway Library Center for the History of Medicine
records.collection: Harvard Embryological Collection and Charles Sedgwick Minot papers
records.type: serial histology collection + original card catalogue/drawings + scientist papers
records.holdings: The Harvard Embryological Collection was created by Charles Sedgwick Minot in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and contains about 2,500 embryo series on about 30,000 microscope slides. The MCZ has preserved and digitised the original card catalogue and associated line drawings and linked them to collection records. Individual MCZbase records expose current catalogue numbers, previous HEC numbers, other identifiers, section plane, stain, thickness, preparator, date, publication citations, and related ledger media. Minot's separate papers at Countway contain correspondence and embryological research notes.
records.research_use: A uniquely explicit serial-section address system. It allows one preparation series to be followed from laboratory preparation and card catalogue through publication citation, old HEC numbering, modern MCZ numbering, digitised ledger documentation, conservation and institutional transfer. It is a major comparator to Cole because seriality here organizes anatomical sequence rather than subscription time.
records.access: MCZ collection and database records are online; original documents have been scanned. Minot papers are open for research at Countway with advance notice.

records.institution: Harvard University — Museum of Comparative Zoology
records.collection: Historical invertebrate microscope-slide collections and digitisation programme
records.type: historical slide collections + labels + current digitisation
records.holdings: The MCZ preserves large invertebrate microscope-slide holdings across Entomology, Malacology and Invertebrate Zoology. Current Harvard documentation highlights nineteenth-century objects including a pseudoscorpion mounted by Nathan Banks in 1891, a William Morton Wheeler slide made for his 1893 insect-embryology thesis, and an older soft-coral slide whose inscription records material sent to James D. Dana by Charles Darwin. Current digitisation work is locating, cleaning, rehousing and cataloguing historically dispersed slides.
records.research_use: A strong case for archival recovery through modern recataloguing. Historical labels can preserve sender, recipient, maker, thesis/publication and locality relations that had become hard to retrieve when slides were dispersed across departmental drawers. Wheeler is especially tractable because an identified 1893 thesis slide can be paired with the printed dissertation.
records.access: Collection pages and selected records are online; digitisation is ongoing and research enquiries can be directed to MCZ Special Collections and relevant departments.

records.institution: University of St Andrews Libraries and Museums — Bell Pettigrew Museum
records.collection: John Thomas Norman zoological microscope slides
records.type: commercial maker slide collection + historical trade catalogue comparator
records.date_scope: nineteenth century with later firm continuation
records.holdings: St Andrews preserves slides carrying the John Thomas Norman name within the Bell Pettigrew Zoology microscope-slide collection. Its collection record explicitly relates the slides to Norman's London mounting business and to his 1872 catalogue of 2,584 microscopic objects. The slides remain dispersed in situ among the collection's slide sleeves rather than being reconstructed as a modern artificial set.
records.research_use: One of the strongest existing catalogue↔surviving-object targets for the trade project. Norman's 2,584-entry printed list can be reversed against surviving labels and subjects to test what catalogue identity remained visible after retail through opticians, secondary labels, private use and later university custody.
records.access: Collection hierarchy and object records online; physical research through St Andrews Libraries and Museums.

records.institution: University of St Andrews Libraries and Museums
records.type: university slide collection + hierarchical storage record
records.holdings: The collection preserves zoological and histological slides created, acquired, contributed and used by staff and students, including William Carmichael McIntosh and D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, together with slides from commercial makers such as Baker, Suter, Enock, Möller and Fritz Meyer. The online archive records the physical hierarchy as slide sleeves, boxes, panels and pigeon-hole positions and notes nineteenth-century slide-size practices.
records.research_use: A strong mixed institutional/commercial endpoint. Its explicit storage hierarchy can be treated as a present address system while maker labels and university actor associations allow reverse searching into trade catalogues, departmental records and the Naples corpus. It also provides a controlled setting in which different maker series coexist after institutional assimilation.
records.access: Collection hierarchy and records are online; research access through University Collections.

records.institution: Whipple Museum of the History of Science, University of Cambridge
records.collection: Mahogany slide case with Pritchard-labelled commercial mounts and homemade preparations
records.type: historical mixed slide cabinet + commercial catalogue labels
records.holdings: The Whipple preserves a brass-bound mahogany case with three lift-out trays containing a mixture of commercial and homemade microscope preparations. The Museum identifies a group of Pritchard mounts whose printed labels derive from his catalogue, alongside broken slides, slide papers and amateur botanical preparations.
records.research_use: An early mixed cabinet that puts commercial catalogue-derived labels, homemade preparations, breakage and paper remnants in one surviving storage object. It is useful for testing how catalogue identities were physically attached to slides before later standardisation and how commercial and amateur preparations cohabited a private cabinet.
records.access: Object record and images online; research access through the Whipple Museum.
